title: At the Hospital
goal: Identify your visit, give important information, ask about a procedure, and report recovery needs.

runs.text: A
department
is a hospital service area.
Outpatient
describes care without an overnight admission under that arrangement.
Admission
here means being accepted into hospital care.
Observation
means monitoring or assessment. An
operating room
is used for surgery;
ICU
, intensive care unit, names a unit providing intensive care. A
ward / unit
is an area for a particular group of patients.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: I have a scan appointment at two thirty under Sam Rivera.

turns.en: I have a scan appointment at two thirty under Sam Rivera.

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: Could I see your confirmation?

turns.en: Could I see your confirmation?

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Here it is. Which department do I need?

turns.en: Here it is. Which department do I need?

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: Imaging. Take this corridor to the reception desk there.

turns.en: Imaging. Take this corridor to the reception desk there.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Is there a step-free route?

turns.en: Is there a step-free route?

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: Yes, I'll show you where the elevator is.

turns.en: Yes, I'll show you where the elevator is.

blocks.caption: Arrive and identify the purpose · Patient & Employee

runs.text: A
scan

is an imaging examination; ask which type if you do not know. For urgent help, say “I need help urgently” and describe the problem rather than waiting to complete a routine appointment script. Ask staff how to reach the appropriate clinical team. Emergency reporting is developed in Chapter 84.

study.title: Share relevant information and ask about assessment

turns.speaker: Nurse

runs.text: When did the pain start?

turns.en: When did the pain start?

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: About two hours ago. I have the names of my regular medicines here.

turns.en: About two hours ago. I have the names of my regular medicines here.

turns.speaker: Nurse

runs.text: Have you had any allergic reactions?

turns.en: Have you had any allergic reactions?

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: I've had a reaction to penicillin. I can describe what happened.

turns.en: I've had a reaction to penicillin. I can describe what happened.

turns.speaker: Nurse

runs.text: Thank you. I'll record that and ask some more questions.

turns.en: Thank you. I'll record that and ask some more questions.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Could you arrange an interpreter? I want to understand the explanation.

turns.en: Could you arrange an interpreter? I want to understand the explanation.

blocks.caption: Share relevant information and ask about assessment · Nurse & Patient

runs.text: Use your actual history in care, not the model's history. “I don't know the medicine's name, but I have the packaging” describes a useful limitation. “Could I call someone?” asks for contact with a support person. “How soon can someone assess me?” asks about the next step without presuming a priority or wait time.

study.title: Understand a proposed stay or procedure

turns.speaker: Clinician

runs.text: We'd like to keep you overnight for observation.

turns.en: We'd like to keep you overnight for observation.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: What are you monitoring, and what would happen next?

turns.en: What are you monitoring, and what would happen next?

turns.speaker: Clinician

runs.text: I'll explain what we know and the plan we're considering.

turns.en: I'll explain what we know and the plan we're considering.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Does that mean surgery is being considered?

turns.en: Does that mean surgery is being considered?

turns.speaker: Clinician

runs.text: Let's discuss that separately so the options are clear.

turns.en: Let's discuss that separately so the options are clear.

blocks.caption: Understand a proposed stay or procedure · Clinician & Patient

runs.text: Surgery / operation
names a procedure involving surgical treatment.
Anesthesia
relates to reducing or preventing sensation during care; different types have different effects. Ask “What type are you proposing?” rather than treating every use as being fully unconscious.
Blood test
temperature
pulse
, and
blood pressure
name assessments you may hear about.

Before a procedure, useful questions are “What is the procedure for?” “What are the alternatives?” “What do I need to know about preparation?” “Who can answer my remaining questions?” “How will pain be managed?” The model does not supply individualized consent, preparation, or treatment advice.

turns.speaker: Nurse

runs.text: How are you feeling now?

turns.en: How are you feeling now?

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Still groggy, and the pain has increased.

turns.en: Still groggy, and the pain has increased.

turns.speaker: Nurse

runs.text: Tell me where it hurts, and I'll contact the team.

turns.en: Tell me where it hurts, and I'll contact the team.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Around the incision. Could someone review it with me?

turns.en: Around the incision. Could someone review it with me?

runs.text: Groggy
means dazed or not fully alert.
Incision
is a surgical cut. “I feel light-headed” reports a feeling of faintness or dizziness. “I need help getting up” describes a need; it does not assert you have permission to walk independently.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Before I leave, could we review the discharge instructions?

turns.en: Before I leave, could we review the discharge instructions?

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: Yes. What would you like clarified?

turns.en: Yes. What would you like clarified?

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: The medicines, follow-up appointment, and who to contact if I notice a problem.

turns.en: The medicines, follow-up appointment, and who to contact if I notice a problem.

turns.speaker: Employee

runs.text: Let's go through those details with the clinical team.

turns.en: Let's go through those details with the clinical team.

turns.speaker: Patient

runs.text: Could I have that information in writing?

turns.en: Could I have that information in writing?

runs.text: Discharge
means release from a care setting under its arrangements;
follow-up
is further contact or care. Ask “Are there any results still pending?”
Pending
means not yet completed or available. For a visitor, ask “What are the visiting hours for this unit?” rather than assuming one rule for the whole hospital.

Fictional role A: Sam Rivera, scan at 2:30, confirmation available, step-free route needed. Role B: pain started two hours ago, medicine list available, prior penicillin reaction. No diagnosis, treatment, or discharge plan is selected.
Check in for Role A. Partner asks for the confirmation. Identify the visit and ask for the route.
Give Role B's history. Partner asks onset, medicines, and reactions. Supply only the stated information.
Partner says overnight observation is proposed. Ask what it involves and whether surgery is being discussed; do not treat one as automatically meaning the other.
Report increased pain during recovery. Ask for review. Then ask three questions about a proposed discharge without inventing medical instructions.
Solo: read the staff prompts and answer out loud, then summarize your own questions with the models hidden. Change the visit type on a later attempt.
Possibilities:

“What are you monitoring overnight?” “I'm still groggy, and the pain is worse.” “Who should I contact after discharge?” Check that the visit, history, current need, and unanswered question are clear. No recovery outcome is guaranteed by the models.
